title: Designing for Real Applications
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of designing for real applications.
Apply user and profile tables in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn designing for real applications through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Designing for Real Applications matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use designing for real applications to make database structure and data rules explicit. Preview changes, name constraints deliberately, consider dependencies, and keep schema evolution in versioned, reviewable scripts.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: User and profile tables, Product and inventory tables, Orders and order items, Payments and transactions. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: User and profile tables
items.text: User and profile tables helps you translate business rules into keys, constraints, normalized schemas, and migration plans that keep invalid data out of the database. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Payments and transactions
items.text: Payments and transactions is about keeping multi-step work correct when errors or other sessions intervene. Keep transactions short, define what must succeed together, handle conflicts explicitly, and test using separate sessions in a disposable database.

items.title: Audit and history tables
items.text: Audit and history tables should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

content_blocks.expected_output: The table combines required values, a range check, and a composite primary key. A production design would also reference student and subject tables with foreign keys.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate designing for real applications using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic user and profile tables and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Designing for Real Applications is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
